title: KV locality entropy + cooperative eviction prototype notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a working note for an experiment cycle that tests a prototype eviction policy designed to exploit temporal locality entropy and cooperative eviction between serving threads. The goal is to reduce tail latencies and page-in churn on high-multiplexing GPU hosts while keeping CPU overhead modest. These are rough results and hypotheses — documenting instrumentation, test matrix, surprising behaviors, and next steps.

Context / motivation:
- Observed repeated tail latency spikes under mixed chat workloads when multiple sessions with different prefix lengths share the same GPU.
- Baseline LRU-style eviction (per-shard) yields acceptable average hit rates, but tail behavior shows heavy page-in activity and NUMA / PCIe stalls when hotsets shift rapidly (canary & burst traffic).
- Hypothesis: Many workloads have skewed reuse but with varying entropy across keys. If we can detect and favor low-entropy (highly-reused) KV entries and run coordinated eviction across workers, we can reduce destructive churn.

Summary of prototype idea:
1) Locality entropy score per KV key: compute an exponentially-weighted moving estimate of reuse-interval entropy. Keys that are reused very frequently get low entropy; unpredictable keys get higher entropy.
2) Cooperative eviction: each serving worker periodically publishes a compact vector (top-k hot keys in its shard with entropy and last-access). A lightweight coordinator computes a global hotset and biases shard-level evictions toward high-entropy keys being evicted first and low-entropy keys being retained.
3) Async background prefetch/evict: when eviction makes room, we trigger nonblocking prefetches for keys predicted to be reused shortly (based on session affinity and Markov-ish short-history). Prefetches are rate limited to avoid saturating PCIe/NVLink.

Experiment matrix (short):
- Hosts: 4x A100-80GB (non-MIG), Ubuntu 22.04, kernels with hugetlbfs enabled on a subset.
- Workloads: 
  * chat-multiplex (40 concurrent sessions, mix of short replies and long context append)
  * long-context-batch (10 sessions, seq_len ~6k, intermittent burst generation)
  * rerank-steady (high embedding traffic, low KV reuse)
- Cache sizes: 16GB, 24GB, 32GB (per-host KV resident working sets)
- Policies compared: baseline-LRU (current), lru-with-prefetch, entropy-coop-evict (prototype), async-paging-to-host (experimental swap-to-host path)
- Measurement windows: 15 minute steady windows after 5 minute warmup.

Instrumentation and signals collected:
- KV hit/miss counters (per key, aggregated into percentiles)
- Per-request token latency (p50/p95/p99)
- Page-in/page-out counts and latency (kernel/mm counters + custom mmap tracing)
- DRAM / GPU memory bandwidth (nvprof/NVML for GPU, perf/pcm for host DRAM)
- PCIe and NVLink transfer bytes per second (from NIC counters and nvlink counters)
- CPU utilization of eviction/coordinator threads (to track overhead)
- Heatmap snapshots: time vs key hotspot intensity (saved as CSVs, referenced in Confluence link)

Key findings (high level):
- Hit rate: entropy-coop-evict improved end-to-end KV hit rate on chat-multiplex by ~9–12 percentage points versus baseline-LRU at 24GB cache size. Baseline: 69% hit, prototype: 80–81% hit. Improvements concentrated on mid-tail keys (access frequency between once per 2–30s).
- Tail latency: p99 token generation latency reduced from ~220ms (baseline) to ~160ms with prototype under the chat-multiplex pattern. p95 improved from ~120ms to ~95ms. Average latency changed minimally (~3–5% improvement).
- Memory bandwidth and page activity: measured host DRAM + PCIe activity on baseline showed ~30% higher page-in events during hotset shifts. Prototype reduced page-in events by ~38% in bursts, and measured PCIe traffic decreased by ~12% across the window. NVLink usage was lower during eviction storms.
- CPU overhead: the cooperative coordinator adds ~3–6% CPU across cores used for serving; eviction scoring and periodic top-k exchange added ~2ms per second of wall-time CPU per worker (low but measurable).
- Adverse case (rerank-steady): when workload has almost no reuse (embedding-heavy, non-repeating keys), prototype overhead slightly worsened latency (~2–4% p95) because prefetch logic mispredicted and caused unnecessary bus traffic. We mitigated this by backing off prefetch when global reuse rate < 15%.

Anecdotes / surprising behaviors:
- Warmup cliff: when many short-lived sessions arrive concurrently (e.g., burst of 200 sessions over 10s), we saw synchronized warmup where many workers attempted to prefetch the same small set of keys leading to a microstorm of PCIe traffic. Adding randomized jitter (spread of 50–200ms) to prefetch solves most of it.
- Cross-shard hotset overlap: for certain prompt templates (e.g., large system prompts shared across customers), the same keys appear as hot across many shards; naive Top-k aggregation made the coordinator think they were globally hot and protected them — which is good — but it also starved some shard-local hot keys. We changed aggregation to prefer keys that appear in multiple workers but include per-shard weight to preserve shard-local balance.
- NUMA sensitivity: on 2-socket hosts with GPUs attached unevenly, eviction decisions that move eviction pressure to the "remote" GPU host caused 20–30ms extra per-token latency due to cross-socket DMA. We added topology-aware scoring to prefer evicting keys with remote affinity first (so remote-affinity keys leave local caches earlier instead of forcing remote reads).

Microbench numbers (representative) - chat-multiplex, 24GB cache:
- Baseline LRU: hit 69.2%, p50 22ms, p95 120ms, p99 220ms, page-ins 1,430 per 15m window
- LRU + prefetch (simple): hit 72.4%, p95 110ms, p99 200ms, page-ins 1,120
- Entropy-coop-evict (proto): hit 80.8%, p95 95ms, p99 160ms, page-ins 880
- Async-page-to-host: hit 78.1% (but page-ins are deferred to host swap, measured swap latency spike risk), p99 310ms in worst cases when swap cold

Interpretation:
- The entropy metric is effective at separating highly-frequency reused rows from bursty/unpredictable rows. By biasing eviction toward high-entropy rows and protecting low-entropy ones, the prototype reduces the destructive eviction of rows that would be reused in the near future.
- Cooperative sharing of hot keys avoids duplicated prefetch/eviction mistakes between workers and can reduce total bus usage.
- Prefetch must be conservative and topology-aware. Over-eager prefetching is the main source of regressions in low-reuse workloads.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Metric tuning: what is the best decay time constant for entropy scoring across chat vs batch workloads? Sensitivity analysis required. (JIRA-REINF-87 task)
- Robustness: induce larger arrival bursts (1k short sessions) and test jitter/backoff strategies more thoroughly.
- Long-run friendliness: evaluate sustained 24h runs to see if long-term drift causes score inflation or starvation.
- Memory accounting: sanity-check accounting when combined with quantized model weights and when using hugetlbfs; ensure kswapd behavior doesn't interfere with predictions.
- Integration with scheduler: could the coordinator be folded into the serving scheduler so routing decisions use cache-awareness? Explore a prototype in serve-runtime router.

Short next steps (engineering):
1) Implement dynamic prefetch-backoff: track global reuse and pause prefetch below a threshold. Target: reduce worst-case regressions in rerank-steady.
2) Add topology-aware weight to the coordinator aggregation (work in branch linked above).
3) Add 24-hour soak and record the entropy distribution drift.
4) Create a small dashboard (Grafana) panel showing per-key entropy histogram and active top-k overlap to help SRE visualize cross-shard hotset overlap.
5) Run experiments with MIG (partitioned GPUs) and smaller per-partition cache sizes to see if the prototype still helps under heavy partitioning.

Notes to self / rough TODOs: 
- Convert heatmaps into CSVs for upload to Confluence link.
- File artifact: /artifacts/kv-proto/run-2025-02-18-heatmap.zip (contains per-window CSVs and pcap-like bus traces).
- Check PR #1428 for the coordinator protobuf change; consolidate field names before merging.
- Remove personal test harness secrets before sharing wider.

Appendix: brief algorithm sketch (pseudocode):
- On access(key): update EWMA inter-arrival (t_i - t_prev), update entropy estimate H_k = alpha*H_k + (1-alpha)*log(interval)
- Periodic (1s): each worker sends top-k keys with (H_k, last_access) to coordinator
- Coordinator: merge top-k, compute global hotset and per-key global_score = f(count_workers, median_H)
- On eviction candidate selection: prefer keys with higher global_score (i.e., higher entropy or low cross-worker count) rather than strictly LRU position
- Prefetch decision: if predicted_reuse_prob(key) > threshold && current_prefetch_rate < budget then issue async prefetch with jitter and record prefetch tag

If you're reading: this is still a prototype; many knobs left to tune. The strongest payoff was the reduction in page-in storms during shifting hotsets. The biggest risks are edge cases with low reuse where prefetching/backpressure causes regressions. Feedback welcome.

-- Nisha
